text.p: Apple Computer Inc. reached back to its roots Tuesday, announcing a broad restructuring that reunites co-founders Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak with the troubled computer maker.

Under the restructuring, Apple said it planned to consolidate its operations into six divisions. Industry analysts said they expected Apple to cut between 2,000 and 3,000 jobs from its workforce of around 13,000 employees.

In a statement that was short of specific details, Apple said it was consolidating the company's product development, marketing, sales support and operations efforts into groups that will focus on core businesses.
Jobs and Wozniak, who founded Apple in 1976 at Jobs' parents home, will serve as advisors to Apple Chairman Gilbert Amelio and serve on Apple's Executive Committee.
Apple, which has been suffering from falling sales of its flagship Macintosh line, said some jobs would be eliminated by the restructuring but it did not provide specifics.
The company said further details would emerge later in the month.
The announcement comes one day before Apple executives meet with shareholders at the company's annual meeting.

"We are reshaping our product development, sales, and marketing efforts into simpler, leaner teams that can quickly bring exceptional products to market -- and then aggressively market them to customers in our key markets," Amelio said.

"The organisation and team we're announcing today represent the right people, in the right places, to bring Apple back to its basics and return us to profitability by the end of the fiscal year," he said.
Apple did not say what it planned to do with its Newton personal digital assistant, which analysts said Apple may decide to sell.

Apple, once the darling of the computer industry, has suffered in recent years from missed opportunities, management turmoil and failed stratgies that resulted in the departures John Sculley in 1993 and Michael Spindler three years later.
Experts say Apple's ill-fated decision not to license the Macintosh operating system to other manufacturers allowed rival Microsoft Corp. to catch up with its Windows operating system.

By the time Apple reversed course, more than 80 percent of the world's computers were using Windows, making it difficult for Apple to make inroads even though many computer enthusiasts felt Apple's system was easier to use.
Compounding Apple's woes were a series of production and forecasting problems that prevented Apple from capitalising on the PC buying craze and the popularity of the Internet.
In its statement, Apple said it planned to integrate its development resources with those of Next Software Inc., which Apple acquired for $400 million. Next was founded by Steve Jobs.

Under Apple's restructuring plan, Ellen Hancock will continue to head up the technology office and the company's product development will be consolidated into two groups, one focusing on system software engineering and the other on hardware engineering.
System Software will be led by Next's Avie Tevanian while Hardware Engineering will be led by Jon Rubinstein, formely chief operating officer of FirePower Systems Inc.
For the first time in Apple's history, marketing operations will be consolidated into a single organisation headed by Guerrino De Luca, formerly the head of Apple's Claris unit.
Apple said Marco Landi will head Apple's new worldwide sales and support organisation and its finance department will continue to be led by Chief Finanical Officer Fred Anderson.

Apple said the new organisation will define and manage the company's upcoming restructuring, which Apple said will include the elimination of programmes and positions. Apple did not specify which programmes would be eliminated. However, it said the restructuring would begin in early March.
Apple stock closed at $15.375, down 94 cents. The announcement was made after the market closed.
